summary: This informational document describes a framework for preventing the transient loops that can occur in link-state routing when topology changes. It does so by correctly ordering the forwarding information base (FIB) updates on routers. It suits planned shutdowns, restarts, and metric changes, and can work alongside fast reroute.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers can briefly disagree about routes after a network change, which can make packets loop. RFC 6976 describes how ordering forwarding-table updates could prevent those temporary loops.

questions: how to avoid micro-loops in link-state routing
how does ofib prevent routing loops
subtitle: An illustrative way to order router updates during topology changes

tldr.problem: During a routing change, routers can temporarily use inconsistent forwarding tables. Packets may loop or be lost while the network converges.
tldr.mechanism: The ordered FIB approach computes an update rank for routers and delays their forwarding-table changes until a safe order is reached. Completion messages can shorten the wait.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6976 describes an illustrative framework, not a protocol specification. It says further work is needed before implementation or deployment of the described mechanism.

facts.label: Failure assumption
facts.value: Loop-free convergence for a single failure

sections.title: Why Routers Can Form Temporary Loops
sections.content:
Link-state routing protocols such as IS-IS and OSPF make routers recalculate forwarding after topology changes. Some routers learn about a change before others, so their forwarding information bases (FIBs) can temporarily disagree. Packets may loop or be lost during this period even when destinations remain reachable in the new topology.

RFC 6976 presents the ordered Forwarding Information Base (oFIB) approach: sequence router FIB updates to maintain consistent forwarding during convergence. It is an illustrative framework and explicitly does not constitute a protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: After a network change, routers may update their forwarding tables at different times. Packets can loop while the tables disagree.

sections.title: The Safe Update Order
sections.content:
For a link-down event or metric increase, a router must wait until routers that send traffic through it and the affected link have updated first. For a link-up event or metric decrease, a router updates before other routers that will use it to reach the changed link.

The same ordering principles extend to router and line-card changes. The RFC assumes that all routers in the routing domain can use oFIB; if routers lack that capability, normal convergence is used.
sections.plainLanguage: When a link goes down, routers using it update before the affected router. When a link comes up, the router that makes the new route usable updates first.

sections.title: Detecting Changes and Computing Rank
sections.content:
Routers collect link-state notifications during a hold-down period to determine whether they describe one event. The approach applies when the notifications share a common router and describe an eligible link-down, link-up, or metric change. If the changes conflict or do not fit the assumptions, a router falls back to conventional convergence.

For an eligible event, each router computes a rank from the topology. The rank determines when it may update its FIB. The RFC gives the update time as T0 + H + (rank × MAX_FIB), where T0 is notification arrival, H is the hold-down time, and MAX_FIB is a network-wide value agreed by the routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers first gather related change notices. Each then calculates a rank that sets its place in the update order.

sections.title: Using Completion Messages
sections.content:
The basic rank timer is conservative. A router can send a completion message after finishing its FIB changes. A router waiting for that neighbor can update as soon as all required completion messages arrive, rather than waiting for its full rank timer.

Completion messages are an optimization only. If a message is lost, the waiting router follows its rank timer, so the ordering does not depend on receiving the message.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can tell its neighbors when its update is complete. Neighbors may then update sooner, while a lost notice only means they wait for their timer.

sections.title: Fallback, Management, and Security
sections.content:
If a router receives a conflicting topology event while ordered convergence is underway, or detects incomplete or inconsistent link-state information, it may abandon oFIB and return to conventional convergence. The RFC discusses candidate methods for coordinating this fallback, called Abandoning All Hope (AAH).

Operators need records of convergence behavior to diagnose it and should study packet reordering caused by delayed updates. The RFC says the framework adds no significant security risks beyond minor routing-protocol changes, but a full analysis belongs in protocol-specific specifications. It also notes that an excessively large timer can delay convergence.
sections.plainLanguage: If new changes break the assumptions, routers return to ordinary convergence. The RFC also calls for operational records and says a full security analysis belongs in later protocol specifications.
